Genome-wide identification and classification of transcription factors in eukaryotic genomes

Fabricio Almeida-Silva

VIB-UGent Center for Plant Systems Biology, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium


Yves Van de Peer

VIB-UGent Center for Plant Systems Biology, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium


2026-10-15

Source: vignettes/vignette_tfhunter.Rmd
vignette_tfhunter.Rmd

Introduction

Transcription factors (TFs) are proteins that bind to cis-regulatory elements in promoter regions of genes and regulate their expression. Identifying them in a genome is useful for a variety of reasons, such as exploring their evolutionary history across clades and inferring gene regulatory networks. tfhunter allows users to identify TFs from whole-genome protein sequences of any eukaryotic species and classify them into families using the classification scheme of CIS-BP. For plants, TFs can also be classified into families and subfamilies (when applicable) using the classification schemes implemented in PlantTFDB and TAPscan, as well as into structure-based families, classes, and superclasses as in Plant-TFClass. Likewise, animal TFs can be classified into structure-based superclasses, classes, and families as in TFClass. tfhunter is the successor of the Bioconductor package planttfhunter. As tfhunter interoperates with core Bioconductor packages (i.e., AAStringSet objects as input, SummarizedExperiment objects as output), it can be easily incorporated in pipelines for TF identification and classification in large-scale genomic data sets.

Installation

You can install tfhunter with the following code:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("tfhunter")

Loading package after installation:

library(tfhunter)

Data description

In this vignette, we will use protein sequences of TFs from the algae species Galdieria sulphuraria as an example, as its proteome is very small. The proteome file was downloaded from the PLAZA Diatoms database (Osuna-Cruz et al. 2020), and it was filtered to keep only genes with TF-related domains for demonstration purposes. The object gsu stores the protein sequences in an AAStringSet object.

Algorithm description

TF identification and classification is based on the presence of signature protein domains, which are identified using profile hidden Markov models (HMMs). Five classification schemes are available, and you can list them with the function list_schemes():

list_schemes()
#>         Scheme             Taxa                    Levels         Annotation
#> 1    PlantTFDB           Plants         family, subfamily          PlantTFDB
#> 2      TAPscan Plants and algae         family, subfamily            TAPscan
#> 3 PlantTFClass           Plants superclass, class, family PlantTFDB, TAPscan
#> 4        CISBP       Eukaryotes                    family              CISBP
#> 5      TFClass          Animals superclass, class, family              CISBP
#>                                                        Reference
#> 1                      Jin et al. (2017), doi:10.1093/nar/gkw982
#> 2                   Petroll et al. (2025), doi:10.1111/tpj.17184
#> 3 Blanc-Mathieu et al. (2024), doi:10.1016/j.tplants.2023.06.023
#> 4         Weirauch et al. (2014), doi:10.1016/j.cell.2014.08.009
#> 5                Wingender et al. (2018), doi:10.1093/nar/gkx987

  1. CIS-BP (Weirauch et al. 2014): TFs from any eukaryotic species are identified based on the presence of DNA-binding domains (DBDs), and they are classified into families defined by the set of DBDs they contain. Each DBD corresponds to a family (e.g., ‘Homeodomain’), and TFs with more than one type of DBD are assigned to a family named after all of them, sorted alphabetically and separated by ‘,’ (e.g., ‘Homeodomain,POU’). As in CIS-BP, DBD hits must have a per-sequence E-value < 0.01 and a per-domain conditional E-value < 0.01, and overlapping hits of different DBDs are resolved by keeping only the most significant hit. This classification rule reproduces the families of all TFs in CIS-BP (build 3.10), and tfhunter classifies TFs into the same CIS-BP families for >98% of the TFs identified by both CIS-BP and tfhunter in species from diverse eukaryotic lineages (yeast, fruit fly, human, Arabidopsis, Phytophthora, and Dictyostelium). Note that CIS-BP’s TF collection also includes some manual curation steps that are not implemented here (e.g., removal of proteins with SANT domains but no Myb domains, and manual curation of human TFs), so tfhunter is expected to identify a few more TFs than CIS-BP.

  2. PlantTFDB (Jin et al. 2017): TFs are classified into families and subfamilies based on DNA-binding, auxiliary, and forbidden domains.

  3. TAPscan v4 (Petroll et al. 2025): transcription-associated proteins (TAPs), which include TFs, transcriptional regulators (TRs), and putative TAPs (PTs), are classified in over 130 families based on rules specifying domains that each family should and should not have. Domain hits are identified using gathering thresholds and domain-specific coverage cutoffs. tfhunter uses an R implementation of TAPscan’s original Perl script, which reproduces the results of the original implementation.

  4. Plant-TFClass (Blanc-Mathieu et al. 2024): TFs are classified into families, classes, and superclasses based on the 3D structure of their DNA-binding domains. Plant-TFClass classifications are inferred from TAPscan classifications using a correspondence table between the two systems. Some TAPscan families correspond to more than one Plant-TFClass family (e.g., TAPscan’s AP2 family includes Plant-TFClass’s AP2, ERF/DREB, and RAV families). In such cases, PlantTFDB subfamilies are used to resolve the ambiguity, and if that is not possible (e.g., because the gene was not classified by PlantTFDB), all possible classifications are reported, separated by ‘;’.

  5. TFClass (Wingender et al. 2018): TFs are classified into superclasses, classes, and families based on the structure of their DNA-binding domains. TFClass includes human TFs and their mammalian orthologs, and TFClass classifications are inferred from CIS-BP families using a correspondence table between the two systems, created by comparing the CIS-BP families and TFClass classifications of human TFs. This approach assigns human TFs to the same TFClass classes as TFClass itself for >99% of the TFs. However, some CIS-BP families correspond to more than one TFClass family (e.g., CIS-BP’s Homeodomain family includes TFClass families HOX, NK, Paired-related HD, and others), so their TFClass family is NA (this is the case for most human TFs). CIS-BP families that do not occur in mammals (e.g., most plant and fungal families) are not classified by TFClass, so this scheme is mostly useful for animals.

In all schemes, classification levels without a more specific level are filled with the name of the more general level. For example, PlantTFDB family bHLH has no subfamilies, so its subfamily is also bHLH, and Plant-TFClass class GRAS has no families, so its family is also GRAS.

The classification schemes are available as data sets in this package, and you can see them below (click to expand).

Identifying and classifying TFs

To identify TFs from protein sequence data, you will use the function annotate_domains(). This function takes as input an AAStringSet object 1 and returns a list of data frames (PlantTFDB, TAPscan, and CISBP) with the protein domains used by each classification scheme. By default, domains are annotated for all classification schemes, but you can choose specific schemes with the argument scheme (e.g., scheme = "CISBP" if you are only interested in CIS-BP and TFClass classifications, which are the only schemes for non-plant species). The HMMER program (Finn et al. 2011) is used to scan protein sequences for the presence of DNA-binding protein domains, as well as auxiliary and forbidden domains. Pre-built HMM profiles can be found in the extdata/ directory of this package. If you have a multicore machine, you can speed up HMMER searches by increasing the number of threads with the argument threads.

Before running annotate_domains(), make sure your protein sequences are suitable for genome-wide TF identification:

Use only one isoform per gene. Proteomes with all isoforms of each gene will result in redundant TFs, as each isoform is treated as a separate gene. We recommend using the translated sequences of the longest (or canonical/primary) transcript of each gene. Note, however, that some TFs could be missed if their DBDs are only present in other isoforms (e.g., 15 human TFs in CIS-BP have DBDs that are only detected in isoforms other than the longest).

Use only proteins encoded by the primary genome assembly. Some proteome files (e.g., the pep.all files from Ensembl) also include proteins encoded by alternative haplotypes and assembly patches, which are copies of genes in the primary assembly. For example, the human proteome in Ensembl includes >100 copies of TFs encoded in alternative haplotypes and patches, which would be identified as additional TFs.

Annotate domains in the whole proteome at once. E-values reported by HMMER depend on the number of sequences that are searched, so domain hits with E-values close to the thresholds may pass or fail filtering depending on the size of the input data set. For consistent results, run annotate_domains() on the whole proteome instead of on subsets of it (e.g., chunks of sequences or candidate TFs only). For the same reason, TFs with E-values close to the thresholds may also differ between tfhunter and CIS-BP, which used different versions of Pfam profile HMMs and proteomes.

This is how you can run annotate_domains() 2:

data(gsu_annotation)

# Annotate TF-related domains using a local installation of HMMER
if(hmmer_is_installed()) {
    gsu_annotation <- annotate_domains(gsu)
} 

# Take a look at the first few lines of the output
lapply(gsu_annotation, head)
#> $PlantTFDB
#>          Gene  Domain qlen c_evalue hmm_from hmm_to
#> 1 gsu144370.1 PF00010   53  2.6e-15        2     50

Now that we have our TF-related domains, we can classify TFs in families with the function classify_tfs().

# Classify TFs into families
gsu_families <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation)

# Take a look at the output
head(gsu_families)
#>         Gene     PlantTFDB_family PlantTFDB_subfamily TAPscan_family

#> 2 gsu04730.1             Nin-like            Nin-like         RWP-RK

The output contains one row per gene, and genes that are not classified by one of the schemes have NA in the respective columns. By default, classify_tfs() uses all classification schemes for which domain annotation is available. As Plant-TFClass classifications are inferred from TAPscan and PlantTFDB classifications, TAPscan and PlantTFDB annotations are required to obtain them. Likewise, TFClass classifications are inferred from CIS-BP classifications. As TAPscan’s scheme also includes other transcription-associated proteins (e.g., transcriptional regulators), more genes are usually classified with TAPscan.

If you are interested in specific classification schemes, you can use the argument scheme to get only the classifications of these schemes. For TAPscan, the class of each family (TF, TR, or PT) is indicated in the column TAP_class.

# Get TAPscan classifications only
tapscan_families <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation, scheme = "TAPscan")
head(tapscan_families)
#>         Gene TAPscan_family TAPscan_subfamily TAP_class
#> 1 AIG92585.1            HAT              GNAT        TR
#> 2 gsu04730.1         RWP-RK               RKD        TF
#> 3 gsu05000.1         RWP-RK               RKD        TF
#> 4 gsu06140.1            MYB       MYB-related        TF
#> 5 gsu06730.1           bZIP              bZIP        TF
#> 6 gsu07030.1            PHD               PHD        TR

# Number of TFs, TRs, and PTs
table(tapscan_families$TAP_class)
#> 
#>  PT  TF  TR 
#>   9 143  96

# Get CIS-BP and PlantTFDB classifications
cisbp_ptfdb <- classify_tfs(gsu_annotation, scheme = c("CISBP", "PlantTFDB"))
head(cisbp_ptfdb)
#>         Gene     PlantTFDB_family PlantTFDB_subfamily CISBP_family
#> 1 gsu04730.1             Nin-like            Nin-like       RWP-RK
#> 2 gsu05000.1             Nin-like            Nin-like       RWP-RK
#> 3 gsu06140.1 GARP;MYB superfamily G2-like;MYB-related     Myb/SANT
#> 4 gsu06730.1                 <NA>                <NA>         bZIP
#> 5 gsu08760.1                 <NA>                <NA>           DM
#> 6 gsu09770.1                  C3H                 C3H         <NA>

TAP classes, as well as descriptions and references for each TAPscan family, are available in the data set tap_class.

data(tap_class)
head(tap_class[, c("TAP_family", "TAP_class")])
#>   TAP_family TAP_class
#> 1   ABI3/VP1        TF
#> 2        AP2        TF
#> 3        ARF        TF
#> 4       ARID        TF
#> 5 Alfin-like        TF
#> 6  Argonaute        TR

Counting TFs per family in multiple species at once

If you want to get TF counts per family for multiple species, you can use the function get_tf_counts(). This function takes a named list of data frames with TF classifications for each species (as returned by classify_tfs()) as input, and it returns a SummarizedExperiment object containing TF counts per family in each species, as well as species metadata (optional). If you are not familiar with the SummarizedExperiment class, you should consider checking the vignettes of the SummarizedExperiment Bioconductor package.

For real data sets, you would first identify and classify TFs in each species. For instance, if you have a list of AAStringSet objects with the proteomes of multiple species 3, you could run:

families <- lapply(proteomes, function(x) classify_tfs(annotate_domains(x)))

To demonstrate how get_tf_counts() works, we will simulate TF classifications for 4 species by sampling 100 random genes from the TF classifications we obtained above (gsu_families) 4 times.

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility

# Simulate 4 different species by sampling 100 random genes 
families <- list(
    Gsu1 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu2 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu3 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ],
    Gsu4 = gsu_families[sample(nrow(gsu_families), 100), ]
)

Now, let’s also create a simulated species metadata data frame for each “species”.

# Create simulated species metadata
species_metadata <- data.frame(
    row.names = names(families),
    Division = "Rhodophyta",
    Origin = c("US", "Belgium", "China", "Brazil")
)

species_metadata
#>        Division  Origin
#> Gsu1 Rhodophyta      US
#> Gsu2 Rhodophyta Belgium
#> Gsu3 Rhodophyta   China
#> Gsu4 Rhodophyta  Brazil

You can add as many columns as you want to the species metadata data frame, but make sure that species names are in row names, and that names(families) match rownames(species_metadata), otherwise get_tf_counts() will return an error.

Now that we have a list of TF classifications and species metadata, we can execute get_tf_counts(). By default, TFs are counted per CIS-BP family, but you can choose other schemes with the argument scheme, and other classification levels with the argument level. Possible levels are ‘family’ and ‘subfamily’ for PlantTFDB and TAPscan, ‘superclass’, ‘class’, and ‘family’ for Plant-TFClass and TFClass, and ‘family’ for CIS-BP (see column Levels in the output of list_schemes()).

# Get TF counts per CIS-BP family in each species
tf_counts <- get_tf_counts(families, species_metadata)

# Take a look at the SummarizedExperiment object
tf_counts
#> class: SummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 20 4 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20): ARID/BRIGHT bHLH ... TCR/CxC Zinc cluster
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(4): Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> colData names(2): Division Origin

# Look at the matrix of counts: assay() function from SummarizedExperiment
SummarizedExperiment::assay(tf_counts)
#>              Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> ARID/BRIGHT     2    3    5    6
#> bHLH            3    2    0    1
#> bZIP           10   12    5   11
#> C2H2 ZF         1    2    0    5
#> CBF/NF-Y        0    0    1    1
#> CSD             0    0    1    0
#> DM              0    0    1    1
#> E2F             1    1    2    0
#> Ets             0    1    1    0
#> GATA            1    1    2    2
#> Homeodomain     2    0    1    0
#> HSF             4    4    3    0
#> MADS box        1    1    1    1
#> Myb/SANT       18   15   23   20
#> RWP-RK          2    4    4    2
#> Sigma 70        1    1    2    1
#> Sox             0    0    1    1
#> TBP             0    0    1    0
#> TCR/CxC         1    1    1    0
#> Zinc cluster    1    2    2    1

# Look at the species metadata: colData() function from SummarizedExperiment
SummarizedExperiment::colData(tf_counts)
#> DataFrame with 4 rows and 2 columns
#>         Division      Origin
#>      <character> <character>
#> Gsu1  Rhodophyta          US
#> Gsu2  Rhodophyta     Belgium
#> Gsu3  Rhodophyta       China
#> Gsu4  Rhodophyta      Brazil

When counting TFs at levels below the highest level of a scheme (e.g., subfamilies), the rowData of the output contains the higher levels of each row, which you can use to aggregate counts. Here is an example with PlantTFDB subfamilies:

# Get TF counts per PlantTFDB subfamily
subfam_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    families, scheme = "PlantTFDB", level = "subfamily"
)

# Look at the family of each subfamily
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(subfam_counts))
#> DataFrame with 6 rows and 1 column
#>         PlantTFDB_family
#>              <character>
#> bHLH                bHLH
#> bZIP                bZIP
#> C2H2                C2H2
#> C3H                  C3H
#> CO-like             C2C2
#> CPP                  CPP

Since get_tf_counts() takes classification tables as input, you can also filter them before counting. For example, here is how you can get counts of TAPscan TFs (excluding TRs and PTs) per subfamily:

# Keep only TFs in TAPscan classifications
tapscan_tfs <- lapply(families, function(x) x[x$TAP_class %in% "TF", ])

# Get TF counts per TAPscan subfamily
tapscan_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    tapscan_tfs, scheme = "TAPscan", level = "subfamily"
)
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(tapscan_counts))
#>           Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> ARID         2    2    3    4
#> bHLH         2    1    0    0
#> bZIP         8   11    5   10
#> C2C2_GATA    1    1    2    2
#> C2H2         2    3    0    4
#> C3H          4    6    2    2

Here is how you can get TF counts per Plant-TFClass superclass:

# Get TF counts per Plant-TFClass superclass
superclass_counts <- get_tf_counts(
    families, scheme = "PlantTFClass", level = "superclass"
)
SummarizedExperiment::assay(superclass_counts)
#>                                             Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> Alpha-helices exposed by beta-structures       1    1    1    1
#> Basic domains                                 10   12    5   10
#> Helix-turn-helix domains                      27   24   33   21
#> Other all-alpha-helical DNA-binding domains    1    1    2    2
#> Yet undefined DNA-binding domains              1    1    1    0
#> Zinc-coordinating DNA-binding domains          3    4    2    6

Here is how you can get TF counts per PlantTFDB family:

# Get TF counts per PlantTFDB family
ptfdb_counts <- get_tf_counts(families, scheme = "PlantTFDB")
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(ptfdb_counts))
#>      Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> bHLH    3    2    0    1
#> bZIP    7    7    2    7
#> C2C2    3    3    7    3
#> C2H2    1    2    0    5
#> C3H     5    6    3    2
#> CPP     1    1    1    0

Finally, here is how you can get TF counts per TFClass class. Note that TFs without a classification at the chosen level (e.g., TFs without a TFClass family when level = "family") are not counted.

# Get TF counts per TFClass class
tfclass_counts <- get_tf_counts(families, scheme = "TFClass", level = "class")
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(tfclass_counts))
#>                                         Gsu1 Gsu2 Gsu3 Gsu4
#> ARID                                       2    3    5    6
#> Basic helix-loop-helix factors (bHLH)      3    2    0    1
#> Basic leucine zipper factors (bZIP)       10   12    5   11
#> C2H2 zinc finger factors                   1    2    0    5
#> Cold-shock domain factors                  0    0    1    0
#> DM-type intertwined zinc finger factors    0    0    1    1

Cool, huh? In real-world analyses, once you have TF counts per family in multiple species obtained with get_tf_counts(), you can try to find associations between TF counts and eco-evolutionary aspects or traits of each species (e.g., higher frequencies of a stress-related TF family in a species that inhabits a stressful environment).
